chunks: "The skin effect is the tendency of alternating current to crowd near the surface of a conductor as frequency goes up.

The reason is electromagnetic induction: a changing current produces a changing magnetic field, and inside the conductor that field induces eddy currents which oppose the current in the center and add to it near the surface.
So at high frequency the current only flows in a thin layer, the skin depth, delta equals square root of over ( pi f micro) . For copper that's about 66 µm at 1 megahertz, 6.
5 µm at 100 megahertz and 2. 1 µm at 1 gigahertz.
The effect is that the usable cross-section shrinks, so the resistance goes up as the square root of frequency, since R proportional to 1 over delta proportional to square root of f .
In transmission lines it's the main conductor loss.
A PCB trace is 35 µm thick with the skin depth falling to 17 µm at about 14 megahertz, and after that the series resistance per length grows as square root of f .
The current also crowds along the surfaces facing the return plane and at the trace edges, which is why making a trace thicker barely helps at GHz, and why rough copper makes things worse.
It also matters for coax center conductors, inductor windings and busbars, which is why people use Litz wire, plated conductors, and smooth copper."
